newsitem.title: USA: U.S. gasoline 'glut' seen amid distillate frenzy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gasoline 'glut' seen amid distillate frenzy.

text.p: U.S. gasoline stocks are poised to swell in coming weeks, a residual effect of European and U.S. refiners' rush to bolster distillate stocks, analysts say.
That could lead to an even sharper decline in gasoline-to-crude margins and hit the bottom line of U.S. refiners.

Tight heating oil inventories in both Europe and the U.S. have spurred an increase in distillate output at both centers. But with refiners limited in how much they can switch production from gasoline to distillates, gasoline is spilling out at a rate too high for seasonally dwindling demand.
Those excess barrels and hefty imports from Europe could equal a glut, analysts said.
"The (U.S.) gasoline market is oversupplied right now," explained Ken Miller of Purvin and Gertz in Houston.
"The incentive is for the refiners to continue running (distillates) like they are right now, and that also produces too much gasoline," he added.

That very scenario has recently sparked a increase in European gasoline exports to the U.S. At least 200,000 tonnes of early October-loading gasoline have been fixed to the East Coast in the U.S. in the past week, and one shipbroker told Reuters that up to five gasoline cargoes have moved.
In the U.S., the heating oil frenzy has produced a similar result, with the only exception that the surplus gasoline barrels will most likely stay put in domestic markets.
U.S. gasoline stocks rose by 2.2 million barrels last week,

according to the American Proleum Istitute. Analysts said that the key to the stock build is a jump in refinery inputs to distillation to 14.7 million barrels a day (bpd) -- 200,000 bpd over last year and 400,000 bpd above the average.
And current indications from refiners points to a mild turnaround season, with the industry maximizing output of distillates throughout the end of October.
"The bottom line is that we know there is an excess capacity to produce gasoline here," Miller stressed. "All the import barrel does is cause it to be worse."
Some analysts questioned how long refiners could sustain their full-throttle attack on the distillate stock deficit.
Although heating oil margins are pleasantly high, they said, returns on spot market gasoline barrels are near nil.
"Just how high are they going to find it economic to crank up yields in distillate runs?" asked John Cooke of the U.S. Energy Department's Energy Infomation Administration.
"Generally when they glut gasoline operations, total refining margins are lower. Surely their planners are looking at the total profit picture and not just the distillate picture," he said.
-- Franklin Paul, New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1620
